summary.statement: The money to solve these crises already exists in the world's annual military budgets. This is not a question of financial capacity. It is a question of political will.

letter.text:
Dear [your head of state],

My name is A concerned citizen. I am writing to you not as a partisan voice, not as an ideologue, and not from a place of anger, but as a human being who has sat with some uncomfortable numbers and can no longer stay quiet about what they mean.

In 2025, the world spent $2.89 trillion on its militaries, the eleventh consecutive annual record. [Pick your country in Step 01 to show what it spends.] I do not write to question the sincerity of those who serve, or to pretend that the threats governments face are not real. I understand that the world is not safe.

But I have come to believe that the world is also not as safe as it could be, precisely because of how we are choosing to spend.

This year, 673 million people went hungry. 272 million children could not go to school. 117.8 million people remain displaced from their homes. The UN's humanitarian appeal received barely a third of what it asked for, while spending on nuclear weapons alone rose 19% to a record $119 billion. These are the compounding conditions of a planet in genuine distress, one that will produce more conflict the longer we leave them unaddressed.

I have thought carefully about where I believe the world must focus its resources. My priorities are:

[Go back, fund some causes and rank them. Your priorities will appear here.]

[Once you have ranked your priorities, the total cost of your choices will be calculated here.]

I am not naive. I know reallocation at this scale requires political courage that is rarely rewarded in short electoral cycles. But the trajectory we are on, ever-increasing military budgets in a warming, hungering, fractured world, is not making any of us safer. It is buying time, not peace.

We are not separate nations with separate interests. We are one species, sharing one atmosphere, drinking from the same water, feeding from the same soil. The decisions made now about how to allocate this planet's resources will shape whether our children inherit a liveable world.

I am choosing to believe you share that goal. And I am asking you, respectfully but urgently, to act like it.

Yours sincerely,

A concerned citizen
[your country]

sections.haveyoursay: Have your say What if we chose differently? Governments hold the budgets, but the public holds the governments. Every figure you have just seen is the result of choices, and choices can change. The money to solve our greatest crises already exists inside one year of military spending. This is not a question of capacity. It is a question of will.
sections.redistribute: Spend the $2.89 trillion on the world instead Tap the causes you'd fund, in order of priority — your most urgent first. The order you choose them in is your ranking. Watch the military budget in the centre drain as you go. SDG 2 Zero Hunger $40B/yr 673 million people faced hunger in 2024. Around $40 billion a year would end it by 2030. The FAO's SOFI report estimates 638 to 720 million people undernourished. UN/FAO and Ceres2030 research puts the additional investment needed to end hunger by 2030 at roughly $37 to 50 billion a year, covering agricultural support, social protection and emergency aid. Former WFP head David Beasley named $40 billion. Hunger is rising sharply across Africa and western Asia. ▾ Read more & sources · 1.4% of the budget FAO ↗ SDG 3 Global Health $371B/yr 4.5 billion people lack full access to essential health services. 2 billion face financial hardship paying for care. WHO's universal health coverage scenario requires 23 million new health workers and 415,000 new facilities. 85% of costs can be met domestically, but the poorest nations face a combined external financing gap of $54B+/year. ▾ Read more & sources · 12.9% of the budget WHO ↗ SDG 4 Quality Education $100B/yr 272 million children and youth are out of school, rising for the seventh year in a row. UNESCO's 2025 dashboard counts 272 million out-of-school children, up 21 million on the previous estimate. Low-income countries spend $55 per learner per year; high-income countries spend $8,543. UNESCO estimates educational gaps cost the global economy $10 trillion a year, and a ~$100B/year investment gap to deliver quality education for all. ▾ Read more & sources · 3.5% of the budget UNESCO ↗ SDG 5 Gender Equality $360B/yr At the current pace, full legal gender parity will not arrive until the 2070s. UN Women estimates $360B/year for meaningful gender equality, legal reform, education access, economic inclusion, reproductive health, and ending gender-based violence. Women and girls bear a disproportionate and largely invisible share of every war's costs. ▾ Read more & sources · 12.5% of the budget UN ↗ SDG 6 Clean Water $114B/yr 2.2 billion people lack safe drinking water. 3.5 billion lack safely managed sanitation. OECD and WHO estimate $114B/year in additional investment closes the global water and sanitation gap by 2030. Waterborne disease kills more children annually than armed conflict. Water stress is among the most reliable predictors of future conflict. ▾ Read more & sources · 3.9% of the budget OECD ↗ SDG 7 Clean Energy $35B/yr ~675 million people have no electricity. Renewables are now the cheapest new power source in most of the world. The IEA estimates just $35B/year in targeted additional investment achieves universal energy access by 2030. The barrier is not technology, it is finance. Countries without reliable electricity cannot build the economic base to invest in any other goal. ▾ Read more & sources · 1.2% of the budget IEA ↗ SDG 8 Decent Work $50B/yr 160 million children remain in child labour. 21 million people in forced labour. The ILO estimates $50B/year in social protection and labour reform would end child labour and forced labour by 2030. Youth unemployment is highest in conflict-affected regions, a direct structural pathway to radicalisation. Decent work is the most effective long-term conflict prevention. ▾ Read more & sources · 1.7% of the budget ILO ↗ $2.89T to redistribute SDG 9 Infrastructure $150B/yr 2.6 billion people lack reliable internet. Billions lack basic transport, energy, and industrial infrastructure. UNCTAD estimates $150B+/year in infrastructure investment for developing nations bridges the connectivity gap and enables growth. Without infrastructure, no other development goal is achievable at scale. ▾ Read more & sources · 5.2% of the budget UNCTAD ↗ SDG 10 Reduce Inequality $150B/yr The richest 1% own more wealth than the bottom 50% of humanity combined. World Bank and Oxfam models indicate $150B/year in social protection floors, progressive redistribution mechanisms, and tax-reform support can materially reduce extreme inequality in developing nations, and the conditions that make conflict inevitable. ▾ Read more & sources · 5.2% of the budget Oxfam ↗ SDG 11 End Homelessness $200B/yr 300 million people have no stable shelter. 1.1 billion live in slums or informal settlements. UN-Habitat estimates $200B/year for a serious global push on affordable housing, building 100,000 new homes every day. Housing precarity is heavily concentrated in post-conflict zones. Stable shelter is the foundation of every other human development indicator. ▾ Read more & sources · 6.9% of the budget UN-Habitat ↗ SDG 13 Climate Action $1.00T/yr The 1.5°C threshold has been breached. Developing nations need $1.3T/year in external climate finance by 2035, they received $116B. At COP29, nations agreed developed countries should mobilise $300B/year by 2035, less than a quarter of what developing countries say they need. The public-finance gap governments must fill is approximately $1T/year. Climate change is a threat multiplier for every other crisis on this list, hunger, conflict, and displacement most of all. ▾ Read more & sources · 34.6% of the budget IPCC ↗ SDG 14 Ocean Health $50B/yr Over a third of fish stocks are at unsustainable levels. Oceans absorb 90% of excess planetary heat. A $50B/year global ocean fund establishes meaningful marine protected areas, ends destructive fishing subsidies, addresses plastic pollution, and funds coral restoration. The ocean generates $2.5T/year in economic value and produces half the oxygen we breathe. ▾ Read more & sources · 1.7% of the budget High ↗ SDG 15 Biodiversity $200B/yr 1 million species face extinction. Species are being lost up to 1,000× faster than natural rates. IUCN and IPBES estimate $200B/year halts and begins to reverse biodiversity collapse. Meanwhile, harmful subsidies to nature-destructive industries total $1.8T/year, nine times what conservation receives. Biodiversity collapse undermines every food and water system on Earth. ▾ Read more & sources · 6.9% of the budget IPBES ↗ SDG 16 Peace & Justice $80B/yr Conflict drives every other crisis on this list. Preventing it is 16× cheaper than responding to it. $80B/year in targeted peacebuilding, institutional reform, anti-corruption, and access to justice would materially reduce new conflicts starting. The cruel irony: money spent here reduces the need for every other investment on this page. The IEP estimates successful diplomacy preventing a single major war is worth trillions. ▾ Read more & sources · 2.8% of the budget IEP ↗ Your priorities, in order use ↑ ↓ to reorder · your top priority first The money to solve these crises already exists in the world's annual military budgets. cards: 1 SDG 2 Zero Hunger $40B/yr 673 million people faced hunger in 2024. Around $40 billion a year would end it by 2030. The FAO's SOFI report estimates 638 to 720 million people undernourished. UN/FAO and Ceres2030 research puts the additional investment needed to end hunger by 2030 at roughly $37 to 50 billion a year, covering agricultural support, social protection and emergency aid. Former WFP head David Beasley named $40 billion. Hunger is rising sharply across Africa and western Asia. ▾ Read more & sources · 1.4% of the budget FAO ↗

2 SDG 3 Global Health $371B/yr 4.5 billion people lack full access to essential health services. 2 billion face financial hardship paying for care. WHO's universal health coverage scenario requires 23 million new health workers and 415,000 new facilities. 85% of costs can be met domestically, but the poorest nations face a combined external financing gap of $54B+/year. ▾ Read more & sources · 12.9% of the budget WHO ↗

3 SDG 4 Quality Education $100B/yr 272 million children and youth are out of school, rising for the seventh year in a row. UNESCO's 2025 dashboard counts 272 million out-of-school children, up 21 million on the previous estimate. Low-income countries spend $55 per learner per year; high-income countries spend $8,543. UNESCO estimates educational gaps cost the global economy $10 trillion a year, and a ~$100B/year investment gap to deliver quality education for all. ▾ Read more & sources · 3.5% of the budget UNESCO ↗

4 SDG 5 Gender Equality $360B/yr At the current pace, full legal gender parity will not arrive until the 2070s. UN Women estimates $360B/year for meaningful gender equality, legal reform, education access, economic inclusion, reproductive health, and ending gender-based violence. Women and girls bear a disproportionate and largely invisible share of every war's costs. ▾ Read more & sources · 12.5% of the budget UN ↗

5 SDG 6 Clean Water $114B/yr 2.2 billion people lack safe drinking water. 3.5 billion lack safely managed sanitation. OECD and WHO estimate $114B/year in additional investment closes the global water and sanitation gap by 2030. Waterborne disease kills more children annually than armed conflict. Water stress is among the most reliable predictors of future conflict. ▾ Read more & sources · 3.9% of the budget OECD ↗

6 SDG 7 Clean Energy $35B/yr ~675 million people have no electricity. Renewables are now the cheapest new power source in most of the world. The IEA estimates just $35B/year in targeted additional investment achieves universal energy access by 2030. The barrier is not technology, it is finance. Countries without reliable electricity cannot build the economic base to invest in any other goal. ▾ Read more & sources · 1.2% of the budget IEA ↗

7 SDG 8 Decent Work $50B/yr 160 million children remain in child labour. 21 million people in forced labour. The ILO estimates $50B/year in social protection and labour reform would end child labour and forced labour by 2030. Youth unemployment is highest in conflict-affected regions, a direct structural pathway to radicalisation. Decent work is the most effective long-term conflict prevention. ▾ Read more & sources · 1.7% of the budget ILO ↗

8 SDG 9 Infrastructure $150B/yr 2.6 billion people lack reliable internet. Billions lack basic transport, energy, and industrial infrastructure. UNCTAD estimates $150B+/year in infrastructure investment for developing nations bridges the connectivity gap and enables growth. Without infrastructure, no other development goal is achievable at scale. ▾ Read more & sources · 5.2% of the budget UNCTAD ↗

9 SDG 10 Reduce Inequality $150B/yr The richest 1% own more wealth than the bottom 50% of humanity combined. World Bank and Oxfam models indicate $150B/year in social protection floors, progressive redistribution mechanisms, and tax-reform support can materially reduce extreme inequality in developing nations, and the conditions that make conflict inevitable. ▾ Read more & sources · 5.2% of the budget Oxfam ↗

10 SDG 11 End Homelessness $200B/yr 300 million people have no stable shelter. 1.1 billion live in slums or informal settlements. UN-Habitat estimates $200B/year for a serious global push on affordable housing, building 100,000 new homes every day. Housing precarity is heavily concentrated in post-conflict zones. Stable shelter is the foundation of every other human development indicator. ▾ Read more & sources · 6.9% of the budget UN-Habitat ↗

11 SDG 13 Climate Action $1.00T/yr The 1.5°C threshold has been breached. Developing nations need $1.3T/year in external climate finance by 2035, they received $116B. At COP29, nations agreed developed countries should mobilise $300B/year by 2035, less than a quarter of what developing countries say they need. The public-finance gap governments must fill is approximately $1T/year. Climate change is a threat multiplier for every other crisis on this list, hunger, conflict, and displacement most of all. ▾ Read more & sources · 34.6% of the budget IPCC ↗

12 SDG 14 Ocean Health $50B/yr Over a third of fish stocks are at unsustainable levels. Oceans absorb 90% of excess planetary heat. A $50B/year global ocean fund establishes meaningful marine protected areas, ends destructive fishing subsidies, addresses plastic pollution, and funds coral restoration. The ocean generates $2.5T/year in economic value and produces half the oxygen we breathe. ▾ Read more & sources · 1.7% of the budget High ↗

letter.text:
Dear [your head of state],

My name is A concerned citizen. I am writing to you not as a partisan voice, not as an ideologue, and not from a place of anger, but as a human being who has sat with some uncomfortable numbers and can no longer stay quiet about what they mean.

In 2025, the world spent $2.89 trillion on its militaries, the eleventh consecutive annual record. [Pick your country in Step 01 to show what it spends.] I do not write to question the sincerity of those who serve, or to pretend that the threats governments face are not real. I understand that the world is not safe.

But I have come to believe that the world is also not as safe as it could be, precisely because of how we are choosing to spend.

This year, 673 million people went hungry. 272 million children could not go to school. 117.8 million people remain displaced from their homes. The UN's humanitarian appeal received barely a third of what it asked for, while spending on nuclear weapons alone rose 19% to a record $119 billion. These are the compounding conditions of a planet in genuine distress, one that will produce more conflict the longer we leave them unaddressed.

I have thought carefully about where I believe the world must focus its resources. My priorities are:

  1. Climate Action ($1.00T per year)
  2. Global Health ($371B per year)
  3. Gender Equality ($360B per year)
  4. End Homelessness ($200B per year)
  5. Biodiversity ($200B per year)
  6. Infrastructure ($150B per year)
  7. Reduce Inequality ($150B per year)
  8. Peace & Justice ($80B per year)
  9. Quality Education ($100B per year)
  10. Clean Water ($114B per year)
  11. Zero Hunger ($40B per year)
  12. Decent Work ($50B per year)
  13. Ocean Health ($50B per year)

To fund all 13 at the levels needed would cost $2.87T per year, about 99% of one year of global military spending. Not a utopian fantasy. A budget question.

I am not naive. I know reallocation at this scale requires political courage that is rarely rewarded in short electoral cycles. But the trajectory we are on, ever-increasing military budgets in a warming, hungering, fractured world, is not making any of us safer. It is buying time, not peace.

We are not separate nations with separate interests. We are one species, sharing one atmosphere, drinking from the same water, feeding from the same soil. The decisions made now about how to allocate this planet's resources will shape whether our children inherit a liveable world.

I am choosing to believe you share that goal. And I am asking you, respectfully but urgently, to act like it.

Yours sincerely,

A concerned citizen
[your country]

letter.text:
Dear Prime Minister / President of United States,

My name is A concerned citizen. I am writing to you not as a partisan voice, not as an ideologue, and not from a place of anger, but as a human being who has sat with some uncomfortable numbers and can no longer stay quiet about what they mean.

In 2025, the world spent $2.89 trillion on its militaries, the eleventh consecutive annual record. United States contributed $954 billion to that total, 3.2% of our national GDP. I do not write to question the sincerity of those who serve, or to pretend that the threats governments face are not real. I understand that the world is not safe.

But I have come to believe that the world is also not as safe as it could be, precisely because of how we are choosing to spend.

This year, 673 million people went hungry. 272 million children could not go to school. 117.8 million people remain displaced from their homes. The UN's humanitarian appeal received barely a third of what it asked for, while spending on nuclear weapons alone rose 19% to a record $119 billion. These are the compounding conditions of a planet in genuine distress, one that will produce more conflict the longer we leave them unaddressed.

I have thought carefully about where I believe the world must focus its resources. My priorities are:

[Go back, fund some causes and rank them. Your priorities will appear here.]

[Once you have ranked your priorities, the total cost of your choices will be calculated here.]

I am not naive. I know reallocation at this scale requires political courage that is rarely rewarded in short electoral cycles. But the trajectory we are on, ever-increasing military budgets in a warming, hungering, fractured world, is not making any of us safer. It is buying time, not peace.

We are not separate nations with separate interests. We are one species, sharing one atmosphere, drinking from the same water, feeding from the same soil. The decisions made now about how to allocate this planet's resources will shape whether our children inherit a liveable world.

I am choosing to believe you share that goal. And I am asking you, respectfully but urgently, to act like it.

Yours sincerely,

A concerned citizen
United States

letter.text:
Dear Prime Minister / President of Samoa,

My name is A concerned citizen. I am writing to you not as a partisan voice, not as an ideologue, and not from a place of anger, but as a human being who has sat with some uncomfortable numbers and can no longer stay quiet about what they mean.

In 2025, the world spent $2.89 trillion on its militaries, the eleventh consecutive annual record. Samoa contributed $0.005 billion to that total, 0.5% of our national GDP. I do not write to question the sincerity of those who serve, or to pretend that the threats governments face are not real. I understand that the world is not safe.

But I have come to believe that the world is also not as safe as it could be, precisely because of how we are choosing to spend.

This year, 673 million people went hungry. 272 million children could not go to school. 117.8 million people remain displaced from their homes. The UN's humanitarian appeal received barely a third of what it asked for, while spending on nuclear weapons alone rose 19% to a record $119 billion. These are the compounding conditions of a planet in genuine distress, one that will produce more conflict the longer we leave them unaddressed.

I have thought carefully about where I believe the world must focus its resources. My priorities are:

[Go back, fund some causes and rank them. Your priorities will appear here.]

[Once you have ranked your priorities, the total cost of your choices will be calculated here.]

I am not naive. I know reallocation at this scale requires political courage that is rarely rewarded in short electoral cycles. But the trajectory we are on, ever-increasing military budgets in a warming, hungering, fractured world, is not making any of us safer. It is buying time, not peace.

We are not separate nations with separate interests. We are one species, sharing one atmosphere, drinking from the same water, feeding from the same soil. The decisions made now about how to allocate this planet's resources will shape whether our children inherit a liveable world.

I am choosing to believe you share that goal. And I am asking you, respectfully but urgently, to act like it.

Yours sincerely,

A concerned citizen
Samoa

letter.text:
Dear TEST,

My name is A concerned citizen. I am writing to you not as a partisan voice, not as an ideologue, and not from a place of anger, but as a human being who has sat with some uncomfortable numbers and can no longer stay quiet about what they mean.

In 2025, the world spent $2.89 trillion on its militaries, the eleventh consecutive annual record. United Kingdom contributed $89 billion to that total, 2.3% of our national GDP. I do not write to question the sincerity of those who serve, or to pretend that the threats governments face are not real. I understand that the world is not safe.

But I have come to believe that the world is also not as safe as it could be, precisely because of how we are choosing to spend.

This year, 673 million people went hungry. 272 million children could not go to school. 117.8 million people remain displaced from their homes. The UN's humanitarian appeal received barely a third of what it asked for, while spending on nuclear weapons alone rose 19% to a record $119 billion. These are the compounding conditions of a planet in genuine distress, one that will produce more conflict the longer we leave them unaddressed.

I have thought carefully about where I believe the world must focus its resources. My priorities are:

  1. Zero Hunger ($40B per year)
  2. Clean Water ($114B per year)
  3. Global Health ($371B per year)

To fund all 3 at the levels needed would cost $525B per year, about 18% of one year of global military spending. Not a utopian fantasy. A budget question.

I am not naive. I know reallocation at this scale requires political courage that is rarely rewarded in short electoral cycles. But the trajectory we are on, ever-increasing military budgets in a warming, hungering, fractured world, is not making any of us safer. It is buying time, not peace.

We are not separate nations with separate interests. We are one species, sharing one atmosphere, drinking from the same water, feeding from the same soil. The decisions made now about how to allocate this planet's resources will shape whether our children inherit a liveable world.

I am choosing to believe you share that goal. And I am asking you, respectfully but urgently, to act like it.

Yours sincerely,

A concerned citizen
United Kingdom

letter.text:
Dear Prime Minister / President of United Kingdom,

My name is A concerned citizen. I am writing to you not as a partisan voice, not as an ideologue, and not from a place of anger, but as a human being who has sat with some uncomfortable numbers and can no longer stay quiet about what they mean.

In 2025, the world spent $2.89 trillion on its militaries, the eleventh consecutive annual record. United Kingdom contributed $89 billion to that total, 2.3% of our national GDP. I do not write to question the sincerity of those who serve, or to pretend that the threats governments face are not real. I understand that the world is not safe.

But I have come to believe that the world is also not as safe as it could be, precisely because of how we are choosing to spend.

This year, 673 million people went hungry. 272 million children could not go to school. 117.8 million people remain displaced from their homes. The UN's humanitarian appeal received barely a third of what it asked for, while spending on nuclear weapons alone rose 19% to a record $119 billion. These are the compounding conditions of a planet in genuine distress, one that will produce more conflict the longer we leave them unaddressed.

I have thought carefully about where I believe the world must focus its resources. My priorities are:

  1. Zero Hunger ($40B per year)
  2. Clean Water ($114B per year)
  3. Global Health ($371B per year)
  4. Quality Education ($100B per year)

To fund all 4 at the levels needed would cost $625B per year, about 22% of one year of global military spending. Not a utopian fantasy. A budget question.

I am not naive. I know reallocation at this scale requires political courage that is rarely rewarded in short electoral cycles. But the trajectory we are on, ever-increasing military budgets in a warming, hungering, fractured world, is not making any of us safer. It is buying time, not peace.

We are not separate nations with separate interests. We are one species, sharing one atmosphere, drinking from the same water, feeding from the same soil. The decisions made now about how to allocate this planet's resources will shape whether our children inherit a liveable world.

I am choosing to believe you share that goal. And I am asking you, respectfully but urgently, to act like it.

Yours sincerely,

A concerned citizen
United Kingdom

letter.text:
Dear Prime Minister / President of United Kingdom,

My name is A concerned citizen. I am writing to you not as a partisan voice, not as an ideologue, and not from a place of anger, but as a human being who has sat with some uncomfortable numbers and can no longer stay quiet about what they mean.

In 2025, the world spent $2.89 trillion on its militaries, the eleventh consecutive annual record. United Kingdom contributed $89 billion to that total, 2.3% of our national GDP. I do not write to question the sincerity of those who serve, or to pretend that the threats governments face are not real. I understand that the world is not safe.

But I have come to believe that the world is also not as safe as it could be, precisely because of how we are choosing to spend.

This year, 673 million people went hungry. 272 million children could not go to school. 117.8 million people remain displaced from their homes. The UN's humanitarian appeal received barely a third of what it asked for, while spending on nuclear weapons alone rose 19% to a record $119 billion. These are the compounding conditions of a planet in genuine distress, one that will produce more conflict the longer we leave them unaddressed.

I have thought carefully about where I believe the world must focus its resources. My priorities are:

  1. Zero Hunger ($40B per year)
  2. Global Health ($371B per year)
  3. Quality Education ($100B per year)
  4. Gender Equality ($360B per year)
  5. Clean Water ($114B per year)
  6. Clean Energy ($35B per year)

To fund all 6 at the levels needed would cost $1.02T per year, about 35% of one year of global military spending. Not a utopian fantasy. A budget question.

I am not naive. I know reallocation at this scale requires political courage that is rarely rewarded in short electoral cycles. But the trajectory we are on, ever-increasing military budgets in a warming, hungering, fractured world, is not making any of us safer. It is buying time, not peace.

We are not separate nations with separate interests. We are one species, sharing one atmosphere, drinking from the same water, feeding from the same soil. The decisions made now about how to allocate this planet's resources will shape whether our children inherit a liveable world.

I am choosing to believe you share that goal. And I am asking you, respectfully but urgently, to act like it.

Yours sincerely,

A concerned citizen
United Kingdom

My name is A concerned citizen. I am writing to you not as a partisan voice, not as an ideologue, and not from a place of anger, but as a human being who has sat with some uncomfortable numbers and can no longer stay quiet about what they mean.

In 2025, the world spent $2.89 trillion on its militaries, the eleventh consecutive annual record. Japan contributed $62 billion to that total, 1.4% of our national GDP. I do not write to question the sincerity of those who serve, or to pretend that the threats governments face are not real. I understand that the world is not safe.

But I have come to believe that the world is also not as safe as it could be, precisely because of how we are choosing to spend.

This year, 673 million people went hungry. 272 million children could not go to school. 117.8 million people remain displaced from their homes. The UN's humanitarian appeal received barely a third of what it asked for, while spending on nuclear weapons alone rose 19% to a record $119 billion. These are the compounding conditions of a planet in genuine distress, one that will produce more conflict the longer we leave them unaddressed.

I have thought carefully about where I believe the world must focus its resources. My priorities are:

[Go back, fund some causes and rank them. Your priorities will appear here.]

[Once you have ranked your priorities, the total cost of your choices will be calculated here.]

I am not naive. I know reallocation at this scale requires political courage that is rarely rewarded in short electoral cycles. But the trajectory we are on, ever-increasing military budgets in a warming, hungering, fractured world, is not making any of us safer. It is buying time, not peace.

We are not separate nations with separate interests. We are one species, sharing one atmosphere, drinking from the same water, feeding from the same soil. The decisions made now about how to allocate this planet's resources will shape whether our children inherit a liveable world.

I am choosing to believe you share that goal. And I am asking you, respectfully but urgently, to act like it.

Yours sincerely,

A concerned citizen
Japan
